questions: How many parts does child A take, and how many does child B take?
How many equal parts is the whole split into?
segments.say: Sharing in a ratio. Show $48 being split for two children in the ratio 2:3 - two parts for A, three parts for B - and name the whole: 5 equal parts. Keep your student notes open at the ratio definition for this scene.

questions: Out of how many parts do we count the 3 parts?
Why can a share of $48 never be $72?
segments.say: Watch out: 3:2 is not 3/2 of the whole. Put the claim on the board and test it against the whole bar: counting 3 parts out of 2 would give $72, more than the $48 we started with, so the parts must be counted out of the 5 parts of the whole.

questions: What is one part worth, and how did you find it?
How much does each child get, and how do you check the shares?
segments.say: One part, then multiply. Five equal parts share $48, so divide: one part is $9.60. Then multiply - two parts is $19.20 for A and three parts is $28.80 for B. Now try the sharing questions on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: What is each share when $48 is shared in 2:3, and what are the three steps?
What goes wrong if we count the parts out of 2 instead of out of 5?
segments.say: The takeaway. Land the rule: add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for each share - A gets $19.20 and B gets $28.80. Finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this trap.
segments.watchFor: A ratio of 3:2 means 3/2 of the whole. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the worksheet: any share of $72 for the 3-part share shows the trap - send them back to scene s3 and to the correct turn: The whole is 5 parts, so 3 parts is 3 fifths of the whole.
